growth_story.headline: US income per person has grown about 1.6 percent a year since 1990, with sharp but short falls in 2009 and 2020 and a firmer last decade.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 the data show one long era: income per person in the United States grew 1.6 percent a year on average over 1990-2025, with no lasting shift up or down. Within that era growth was strong in the late 1990s, reaching 3.6 percent in 1999. The IMF traces the boom of the mid-2000s to a credit-fuelled housing bubble, and after the bust income per person fell 3.4 percent in 2009. Over 2006-2015 growth averaged only 0.8 percent a year, after the IMF had warned in 2009 that households repairing their finances would weigh on growth. The pandemic cut income per person by 2.5 percent in 2020, but it bounced back 6.0 percent in 2021, and the IMF found no lasting scar. Over 2016-2025 growth averaged 1.8 percent and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025; the IMF credits growth in 2025 to strong productivity growth, while the OECD describes a longer slowing tied to weaker productivity growth and an ageing population.

threads.title: Housing bust and financial crisis
threads.text: In the mid-2000s a credit-fuelled housing bubble pushed up house prices, and rising housing wealth fed spending. After the bust, income per person fell 3.4 percent in 2009. In 2009 the IMF expected households' repair of their finances to hold growth back for years, and growth over 2006-2015 averaged 0.8 percent.

threads.title: Pandemic fall and fast rebound
threads.text: Income per person fell 2.5 percent in 2020 and rose 6.0 percent in 2021. By 2024 the IMF found that output and jobs had passed the levels expected before the pandemic, so the shock left no lasting scar.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2024 Article IV Consultation with the United States
citations.quote: Hysteresis effects from the pandemic did not materialize; both activity and employment now exceed pre‑pandemic expectations.

threads.title: Productivity and an ageing population
threads.text: The OECD describes a long fall in productivity growth since the early 1990s, along with signs of weaker competition and an ageing population. More recent IMF reports paint a different picture for 2025, when continued strong productivity growth drove the economy.

threads.text: After the pandemic, a wave of immigrant workers added to the labor force and helped soften the effect of higher interest rates. In 2025 that inflow fell sharply, and the IMF links slower job growth partly to lower immigration.

threads.text: By 2024 the OECD found that trade policy had become restrictive. In 2026 the IMF said higher tariffs create costs by distorting how resources are used and disrupting supply chains, even as growth held up in 2025 through major policy shifts and a government shutdown.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 income per person grew 1.6 percent, and the IMF notes that growth held up through major policy shifts and a government shutdown. In September 2026 the OECD reported that investment in data centres and technology equipment, tied to artificial intelligence, lifted US growth in the second quarter. Over the same period energy prices rose again worldwide as disruptions in the Gulf economies deepened.

growth_story.tension: The OECD describes a long structural slowing in growth and a fall in productivity growth since the early 1990s. Yet the data on income per person show no lasting shift since 1990 (1.6 percent a year), and the last decade (1.8) ran faster than the one before (0.8).
